plan.chapterName: OpenStax University Physics, chapter 6: Applications of Newton's Laws
plan.contextChunk: This figure combines a pictorial diagram with two force diagrams drawn beside it. At the left, a pulley hangs on a short stem from a beige ceiling beam; its gray grooved wheel carries a yellow cord whose two ends drop vertically to a pair of wood-grain square blocks, the higher one at the left labeled m1 and the lower one at the right labeled m2. To the right, under the headings "Block 1" and "Block 2", each block is redrawn alone as the same wood-grain square with a red vector T pointing straight up from its top edge and a red weight vector pointing straight down, labeled w1 and w2 respectively. The two tension arrows are drawn the same length, while the downward arrow on block 2 is noticeably longer than the one on block 1. Keeping the tension arrows identical while letting the weight arrows differ is the comparison the reader is meant to make. The figure sets up the Atwood machine, in which two unequal masses joined over a frictionless pulley share one string tension and accelerate equally in opposite directions.

interactionPlan.concept: In an Atwood machine, two unequal masses joined by one string over a frictionless pulley share a single tension and accelerate with equal magnitude in opposite directions, driven by the difference in their weights.
elements: beige ceiling beam at top with pulley mounting stem
gray grooved pulley wheel with hub
yellow cord draped over the pulley, both ends hanging vertically
wood-grain square block m1 (higher, left side), labeled m1
wood-grain square block m2 (lower, right side), labeled m2
free-body panel labeled 'Block 1': wood-grain square, red upward tension vector T, red downward weight vector w1
free-body panel labeled 'Block 2': wood-grain square, red upward tension vector T (same length as Block 1's), red downward weight vector w2 (longer than w1)
green acceleration arrows on each block (a up on m1, a down on m2, equal length), shown after release

interactions.label: Mass m2 (m1 fixed)
interactions.teaches: The two tension arrows stay equal no matter how the masses change — only the weight arrows and the resulting acceleration grow with the mass difference, so unequal weights cause the motion while one tension acts on both blocks

interactions.label: Release the blocks
interactions.teaches: Once released, the heavier block descends and the lighter block rises by exactly the same distance in the same time — the connecting string forces equal-magnitude, opposite-direction accelerations

demo_steps.title: One string, one tension
demo_steps.narration: Compare the two free-body diagrams: both tension arrows are identical in length because a single string carries the same tension to both blocks, while w2 is longer than w1 because m2 is heavier.

demo_steps.title: Change the mass difference
demo_steps.narration: Drag the m2 slider: the weight arrows and the acceleration arrows resize together, but the two tension arrows remain equal — the mass difference sets how fast the system accelerates, not whether the tensions match.

demo_steps.title: Release and watch the motion
demo_steps.narration: Step from held to released to moving: m2 sinks while m1 rises by the same amount, showing the string constraint — equal-magnitude accelerations in opposite directions.

demo_steps.title: Balanced masses
demo_steps.narration: Set m2 equal to m1: the weight arrows match, acceleration drops to zero, and the blocks hang motionless even after release — acceleration comes only from the weight difference.

interactionPlan.keyInsight: A single string enforces a single tension and a single acceleration magnitude on both blocks; only the difference in weights drives the motion, so equal masses mean zero acceleration.
interactionPlan.reconstructionNotes: Left panel: beige ceiling beam, gray pulley on a short stem, yellow cord hanging vertically on both sides to wood-grain square blocks — m1 higher on the left, m2 lower on the right. Right panel: two free-body diagrams side by side under headings 'Block 1' and 'Block 2', each a wood-grain square with a red upward T arrow from the top edge and a red downward weight arrow (w1, w2) from the bottom edge; tension arrows always drawn equal length, w2 longer than w1 by an amount tracking the slider. Acceleration arrows (distinct color, e.g. green) appear on the blocks in the released/moving states, pointing up on m1 and down on m2 with equal lengths that scale with the mass difference. In the moving state, animate block positions: m2 descends and m1 rises by equal distances, cord sliding over the pulley. Keep arrow lengths proportional and clearly comparable across the two free-body diagrams — the equal tensions versus unequal weights is the central visual comparison.

authoredContext:
Atwood Machine A classic problem in physics, similar to the one we just solved, is that of the Atwood machine, which consists of a rope running over a pulley, with two objects of different mass attached. It is particularly useful in understanding the connection between force and motion. In the figure, m1=2.00kg and m2=4.00kg. Consider the pulley to be frictionless. (a) If m2 is released, what will its acceleration be? (b) What is the tension in the string?

T=2m1m2m1+m2g (This is found by substituting the equation for acceleration in the figure(a), into the equation for tension in the figure(b).)

An Atwood machine and free-body diagrams for each of the two blocks.

An Atwood machine consists of masses suspended on either side of a pulley by a string passing over the pulley. In the figure, mass m sub 1 is on the left and mass m sub 2 is on the right. The free body diagram of block one shows mass one with force vector T pointing vertically up and force vector w sub one pointing vertically down. The free body diagram of block two shows mass two with force vector T pointing vertically up and force vector w sub two pointing vertically down.

Strategy We draw a free-body diagram for each mass separately, as shown in the figure. Then we analyze each diagram to find the required unknowns. This may involve the solution of simultaneous equations. It is also important to note the similarity with the previous example. As block 2 accelerates with acceleration a2 in the downward direction, block 1 accelerates upward with acceleration a1. Thus, a=a1=−a2.

discrepancies: the source marks forces with vector notation (T⃗ and w⃗ with overhead arrows); the generated figure uses plain 'T', 'w₁', 'w₂' text without the vector accents

the pulley and support are heavily simplified — the source shows a yoke bracket, grooved rim, hub and mounting bolts, while the generated version is a plain gray disk with spokes hanging from a simple plate
the 'moving' state oscillates both blocks sinusoidally up and down, whereas a released Atwood machine accelerates in one direction (m₂ down, m₁ up) until it hits a limit
in the source the weight arrows emanate from the block centers and pass through the bottom edge; the generated arrows begin at the bottom edge
evaluation.notes: Composition, colors, and the core physics (equal red tension arrows, mass-scaled weight arrows, m₁ high / m₂ low) match the source well, and the slider, release animation, and 4-step demo are all functional and on-concept; the main weaknesses are the non-physical oscillating motion, missing vector-arrow notation on the force labels, and a noticeably simplified pulley.
action_items: Replace the sinusoidal 'moving' animation with one-directional constant-acceleration motion (m₂ descending, m₁ rising) that clamps or resets at travel limits, so the dynamics don't imply the system oscillates.
Render the force labels with vector arrows over the glyphs (T⃗, w⃗₁, w⃗₂) to match the source notation.
Add pulley detail — a bracket/yoke over the wheel, a darker rim groove for the cord, and a distinct hub — to better resemble the source hardware.
Start the weight arrows at the block centers (passing through the bottom edge) as in the source free-body diagrams.
